domains.name: Essay & Examination Genres
domains.summary: This domain covers the essay, examination, review and source-based genres most often assessed in foundation, pre-sessional and taught programmes, including the extended source-based project that caps many pre-sessional and foundation courses, together with the genre concepts and analytic strategies learners need to handle genres they have not been explicitly taught. Comparison, explanation and problem–solution essays are treated as rhetorical patterns within the essay family rather than as separate genres, and each genre topic integrates component skills from the writing, sources, argument, discourse and reading strands. Because conventions vary by discipline, department and assignment brief, every topic stresses analysis of local exemplars, briefs and marking criteria rather than a single template; the domain draws on the ESP, Sydney School and New Rhetoric genre traditions and on corpus evidence about genre families in UK student writing.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what different kinds of university writing are for, how they are organised and what language they use, and how to study examples so you can handle new tasks.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Discussion and expository essays, summary–response and short answers with strong scaffolding, building towards a guided extended source-based project and the idea that texts are shaped by purpose and reader.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: The move from test-style opinion essays to source-based argumentative essays and annotated bibliographies, culminating in the extended project, with a map of the genre families met in the first year of a degree.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Source-based argument, article critiques and annotated bibliographies feeding an extended project with a short review of literature, plus independent analysis of exemplars from the target master's programme.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific essays, exam essays, critiques and reflective writing worked through real module briefs, criteria and feedback, with coursework literature reviews in later years.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid adaptation to coursework literature reviews, critiques, reflective and exam genres within a compressed year, with independent genre analysis as the transferable skill.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Genre analysis as an independent research skill and book reviews as early publications; doctoral genres themselves sit in the Research Communication strand.

domains.name: Report & Practice-Based Genres
domains.summary: This domain covers report-based, practice-based and professional genres in which students document investigations, analyse cases, justify designs, propose projects, summarise for decision-makers, reflect on practice and write for non-academic readers. Most are discipline-specific in their sections, terminology and evidence, so each topic sets out common purposes, stages and language while stressing that lab manuals, templates, handbooks and assignment briefs override any generic model. The domain draws on genre-family research on UK student writing, analyses of particular student genres such as the lab report and the business case report, and research on reflective writing.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how reports, case studies, proposals, portfolios and dissertations work and what their readers need, and how to follow your own department's templates and expectations.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Report conventions, guided lab reports and introductory case studies and business reports in subject pathways.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Report conventions and, in subject-specific strands, short lab, case or business reports; the extended project may itself take report form.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Report formats for the target discipline, such as business, case or small empirical project reports, and in some programmes a short taught-programme project proposal.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-embedded lab, design, business and case reports, placement portfolios and the final-year dissertation or project.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: The dissertation proposal and the master's dissertation, alongside professional reports, case analyses, policy briefs and portfolios, often within a compressed timeline.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Policy briefs and public-facing writing for engagement and impact; doctoral proposals and theses sit in the Research Communication strand.

topics.name: What a genre is
topics.description: Understand a genre as a recognisable, purpose-driven type of communicative event (an essay, a lab report, a case study, an email to a tutor) whose typical stages, content and language are shaped by the shared purposes and expectations of a discourse community. Seeing conventions as motivated responses to purpose, reader and context, rather than as arbitrary rules, lets learners explain why texts differ across modules and adapt to genres they have not been taught.
masteryEvidence: Explains, with reference to purpose and reader, why two texts on the same topic written in different genres differ in staging and language
Identifies the likely discourse community, readers and communicative purpose of an unfamiliar academic text
Distinguishes a genre (a socially recognised text type such as a case study) from a rhetorical function or text type used within it (such as explaining or comparing)
Recognises that conventions for a named genre vary across disciplines, departments and assignment briefs, and names the local evidence that would settle a question about them
Uses genre terms (purpose, audience, stage or move, convention) accurately when discussing their own and others' texts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner the opening paragraphs of two texts on the same topic, one from a student lab report and one from a popular science article. Ask them to explain three differences and why each exists. A secure response attributes the differences to purpose, reader and context rather than to 'formality' alone, and does not claim that one text is simply more correct.

topics.name: Analysing genres independently
topics.description: Analyse exemplars of a target genre, alongside the assignment brief and marking criteria, to identify its purpose, stages or moves, typical content and characteristic language, and turn these observations into decisions for one's own text. This rhetorical consciousness-raising lets learners master genres an EAP course cannot cover and protects them against a generic model that the local department does not use.
masteryEvidence: Segments an exemplar into functional stages or moves and labels each by what it does for the reader, not by its topic
Identifies recurrent language associated with particular moves, such as tense, hedging, citation pattern or metadiscourse
Compares two or more exemplars to separate apparently conventional features from optional or writer-specific choices
Triangulates exemplar analysis with the assignment brief, marking criteria and tutor guidance before generalising
Explains how a specific feature of their own draft follows from the analysis
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short exemplar of a genre the class has not studied (for example a 250-word conference abstract or the introduction to a module case study). Ask them to divide it into moves, label each by function and name one language feature per move. Check whether labels are functional ('justifies the method') rather than topical ('about the sample'), and whether the learner cautions against generalising from a single exemplar.

topics.name: Genre families and essay types in university assessment
topics.description: Know the range of genre families in which students are assessed (essays, critiques, explanations, exercises, case studies, literature surveys, methodology recounts such as lab reports, research reports, proposals, design specifications, problem questions, narrative or reflective recounts, and empathy writing for non-specialist or professional readers) and, within the essay family, the main essay types (exposition or argument, discussion, factorial and consequential explanation, comparison, problem–solution and challenge or commentary essays), together with how each purpose shapes the thesis, organisation and conclusion. This map helps learners recognise what an assignment is asking for, see that the essay is not the dominant genre in many disciplines, and plan for questions that blend types; labels vary across departments, courses and textbooks, so the brief and criteria outrank any label.
masteryEvidence: Classifies a set of real assignment briefs by genre family and states the social purpose each serves
Identifies the essay type or types a question implies and explains how that purpose shapes the thesis and structure, rather than mapping command words mechanically to templates
Distinguishes a discussion essay that weighs perspectives towards a judgement from an argumentative essay that defends a position from the outset, and recognises the continuum between them
Recognises when a question combines types (for example explaining and then evaluating) and plans a structure that serves both
Identifies which genre families predominate in their own discipline and level of study
Recognises when an assignment label names one genre but the brief and criteria require features of another, and seeks clarification
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner six anonymised briefs from different disciplines and four essay questions on one topic with different focuses. Ask them to sort the briefs into genre families and to sketch, in three lines each, the structure each essay question implies. Check that sorting rests on purpose and expected structure rather than subject or title, that the essay outlines differ for principled reasons, and that a blended question is recognised.

topics.name: Argumentative essay
topics.description: Produce a thesis-led essay that takes a defensible position on a contested question and builds a cumulative, source-supported case for it, engaging with alternative views and qualifying the position where the evidence requires. Typical stages are an introduction that frames the issue and states the thesis, body paragraphs that each advance a reason with evidence and commentary, treatment of counter-positions, and a conclusion that answers the question in the light of the argument; characteristic language includes stance markers, hedges and boosters, concession–counter patterns and evaluative reporting of sources.
masteryEvidence: States a specific, arguable thesis that directly answers the question and develops it, rather than merely repeating it, across the essay
Orders body paragraphs so that each sub-claim contributes to the overall case, with explicit links back to the thesis
Supports claims with relevant, attributed source evidence and explains how the evidence supports each claim
Represents at least one serious counter-position fairly and concedes or rebuts it with reasons
Calibrates claim strength to the evidence with hedges and boosters
Writes a conclusion that answers the question and states the limits or implications of the position
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an essay question and 20 minutes to produce a thesis statement, three topic sentences and one counter-argument with a response. Check that the thesis takes a position, that the topic sentences advance distinct reasons for it rather than naming topics, and that the counter-argument is a credible objection answered with a reason rather than dismissed.

topics.name: Discussion essay
topics.description: Produce an essay that represents two or more perspectives on an issue fairly, weighs them against evidence and explicit criteria, and reaches a reasoned, qualified conclusion. Typical stages are statement of the issue, presentation of perspectives (in blocks or point by point), evaluation and judgement; characteristic language includes attribution and reporting verbs, contrastive connectors, concession and evaluative lexis. In UK higher education even a 'discuss' essay is usually expected to arrive at a position, and often to signal it early.
masteryEvidence: Represents each perspective accurately and with comparable care, attributing views to their sources
Organises perspectives point by point or in blocks and can justify the choice
Evaluates perspectives against explicit criteria or evidence rather than simply juxtaposing them
Keeps their own evaluation linguistically distinguishable from reported views
Reaches a conclusion that follows from the weighing and is appropriately qualified
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 'Discuss' question and two short sources holding opposing views. Ask for an outline plan and the concluding paragraph. Check that the plan includes an evaluative stage, that both views are represented fairly, and that the conclusion takes a qualified position derived from the weighing rather than stating that both sides have advantages.

topics.name: Expository essays organised by rhetorical pattern
topics.description: Produce essays, or essay sections, whose organisation is driven mainly by one rhetorical pattern: explanation of causes, consequences or a mechanism; comparison of theories, cases, methods or policies against explicit criteria; or problem–response–evaluation leading to a justified recommendation. These are treated as patterns used within the essay family (and inside explanations, case studies and reports) rather than as separate genres, because departments rarely name them and real questions often combine them; each pattern still needs a controlling claim that says what the explanation, comparison or evaluation shows. The topic builds on the corresponding rhetorical functions (cause and effect, comparing and contrasting, problem–solution and evaluating), adding whole-text staging, source support and calibrated claims.
masteryEvidence: Identifies whether a question calls mainly for explanation (causes, consequences or mechanism), comparison or problem–solution, or a combination, and plans the structure accordingly
States a controlling claim that says what the explanation, comparison or evaluation shows rather than announcing the topic
Organises the body consistently by factor, by criterion (point by point, or in blocks with explicit cross-reference) or by problem–response–evaluation, and justifies the order
Explains mechanisms, the significance of differences or the trade-offs between responses rather than listing causes, features or solutions

Uses the pattern's signalling language accurately, including causal verbs and nouns, comparative structures and contrastive connectors, problem and evaluation nouns, and conditional and recommending forms
Supports points with cited source evidence and hedges causal and predictive claims to suit the evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three questions on one topic that call for different patterns (for example 'Explain why…', 'Compare… as approaches to…', 'Evaluate responses to…') and a short source pack. Ask for a thesis and paragraph plan for each and one full body paragraph for one of them. Check that the plans differ in organisation for principled reasons, that each thesis states an outcome rather than a topic, and that the paragraph explains a mechanism, the significance of a difference or a criterion-based evaluation, with cited evidence and calibrated claims.

topics.name: Examination essay
topics.description: Write an essay under timed, usually closed-book conditions that answers the set question directly from revised knowledge, with a clear position, a quickly planned structure and selective use of remembered evidence. Compared with coursework essays, examiners typically expect a compact introduction, sustained relevance and less precisely referenced sources; expectations about citation, length and structure vary by department and should be checked in past papers, examiners' comments and module guidance.
masteryEvidence: Decodes the question's command words, scope and implied structure within the first minutes and plans accordingly
Allocates time across questions in proportion to marks and leaves time to check
States a direct answer to the question in the introduction and returns to it in each paragraph
Selects revised content that serves the argument rather than reproducing everything remembered
Refers to scholars, theories and evidence with the degree of precision expected locally in exams (for example author and approximate date)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Set an unseen question from a past paper in the learner's subject area with 40 minutes' writing time. Check the first paragraph for a direct answer, whether body paragraphs stay relevant to the question rather than reproducing pre-learned material, and whether the essay is complete and visibly planned.

topics.name: Short-answer responses
topics.description: Write concise, accurate answers, from a sentence to a paragraph, that define, identify, explain or briefly justify, as required in coursework exercises, short-answer exam questions and in-class tests. Markers reward precision, correct terminology and completeness relative to the marks available rather than introductions or elaboration; typical language includes formal definitions, compact causal and procedural explanation, and dense noun phrases.
masteryEvidence: Answers the question in the first sentence without restating it or adding an introduction
Scales the length and number of points to the marks available
Uses discipline terminology accurately and gives formal definitions where the question requires them
Includes the explanation step (how or why) when the command word requires more than identification
Adds an example or brief evidence only where it earns credit
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three short-answer questions worth 2, 4 and 6 marks on content they have studied. Check whether answer length and number of points scale with the marks, whether the first sentence answers directly, and whether 'explain' items include a reason or mechanism rather than a bare identification.

topics.name: Critical review of an article
topics.description: Write a review of a single research article or theoretical text that summarises its aims, approach and main claims accurately and concisely, then evaluates it against appropriate criteria (such as quality of evidence, methodological soundness, coherence of argument, contribution and relevance) and reaches a balanced overall judgement. Typical stages are context and purpose, summary, evaluation of strengths and limitations, and conclusion; characteristic language includes evaluative reporting verbs, mitigated criticism, praise–criticism pairs and hedged judgements.
masteryEvidence: Summarises the text's purpose, approach and main claims accurately, in the proportion the brief requires
Evaluates against explicit criteria suited to the text type rather than personal agreement or disagreement
Supports each evaluative point with specific reference to the text and, where useful, to other literature
Balances strengths and limitations and mitigates criticism appropriately
Reaches an overall judgement about the text's value for a stated purpose or reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstract and methods section of a short empirical article and ask for one evaluative paragraph. Check that the evaluation targets a specific feature (for example the sample or a measure), explains its consequence for the authors' claims, and is phrased with appropriate mitigation rather than as dismissal or unexplained praise.

topics.name: Book review
topics.description: Write a review of a scholarly book for an academic readership that situates the book in its field, describes its aims, scope and structure selectively, evaluates its argument, evidence and contribution, and recommends it, or not, to specified readers. Unlike an article critique set as coursework, a published book review is a public evaluative act within a discipline: reviewers balance and often mitigate criticism, and follow venue conventions on length, structure and bibliographic header.
masteryEvidence: Situates the book in relation to its field and the debates it addresses
Describes the book's aims and structure selectively, foregrounding what the evaluation needs
Evaluates contribution, argument and evidence with specific reference to chapters or claims
Balances praise and criticism and mitigates criticism to suit the venue
Identifies the intended readership and recommends the book to them with reasons
Follows the conventions of a target journal or brief for length, headings and bibliographic details
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give learners two published book reviews from a journal in their field. Ask them to mark where the reviewer evaluates, how criticism is softened and to whom the book is recommended, then to write the closing recommendation paragraph for a book they know. Check for a balanced, reasoned judgement addressed to a specified readership.

topics.name: Reflective writing
topics.description: Write structured reflection that describes a significant experience selectively, examines one's responses and assumptions, analyses the experience using relevant theory or evidence, and draws conclusions for future practice or learning. Assessed in education, health, business, engineering and EAP itself, the genre combines first-person, past-tense recount with present-tense analysis and future-oriented action planning; markers usually reward depth of analysis and links to theory rather than description or disclosure, and briefs differ widely on structure and citation.
masteryEvidence: Selects a specific, significant incident and describes it concisely as a basis for analysis
Moves from description to analysis by explaining why events unfolded as they did and questioning their own assumptions
Links the experience to relevant theory, research or professional standards
Uses first person, tense shifts and hedged interpretation appropriately across reflective stages
Formulates specific, realistic actions for future practice that follow from the analysis
Uses a reflective model as a scaffold without letting it dictate a formulaic text, following the local brief on structure
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two short reflective paragraphs on the same incident, one largely descriptive and one analytical. Ask which would gain higher marks and why, then ask them to add two sentences to the weaker one. Check whether the additions interpret the experience, link it to theory or evidence, or derive a future action, rather than adding narrative or emotion.

topics.name: Annotated bibliography
topics.description: Compile an annotated bibliography in which each correctly formatted reference is followed by a concise annotation that summarises the source's purpose, approach and main findings or argument and, depending on the brief, evaluates its quality and explains its relevance to the writer's project. The genre isolates and trains selective summarising, source evaluation and relevance judgement; annotations are usually short paragraphs, report the source's claims with present-tense reporting verbs and mark evaluative and relevance comments as the writer's own.
masteryEvidence: Formats each entry accurately in the required referencing style
Summarises each source's purpose, approach and key claims concisely without reproducing its abstract
Evaluates each source with explicit criteria suited to its type (for example authority, evidence, currency)
Explains how each source will be used in the writer's project where the brief requires it
Keeps descriptive, evaluative and relevance comments distinguishable within each annotation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a journal article (or its abstract and methods) and a stated project focus, and ask for an annotation of about 150 words. Check that the annotation does not reproduce the abstract, includes a reasoned evaluation, states relevance to the project and is preceded by an accurate reference.

topics.name: Literature review assignment
topics.description: Write a coursework literature review, stand-alone or as a section of a larger assignment, that maps and synthesises the literature on a defined question thematically, evaluates the strength and limits of the evidence, identifies agreements, tensions and gaps, and positions a question or argument in relation to them. Typical stages are scope and rationale, thematic sections in which sources are placed in dialogue, and a conclusion summarising the state of knowledge and its gaps; characteristic language includes varied integral and non-integral citation, evaluative reporting verbs, comparison, and the present perfect for the state of a field. This topic covers coursework reviews set on taught programmes (pre-sessional PG, undergraduate and taught master's modules); the review that positions the writer's own study in a thesis, article or dissertation chapter is res.literature-review, which normally builds on this one.
masteryEvidence: Defines and justifies the scope of the review and, where required, the search approach
Organises the review by themes, debates or methods rather than source by source
Synthesises several sources within paragraphs, showing agreement, disagreement and qualification
Evaluates the evidence base rather than only reporting it
Identifies gaps or tensions that follow from the review and states their significance for the question
Maintains authorial voice through topic sentences and commentary that frame the cited material
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give learners five short source summaries on one question and 25 minutes to write one synthesis paragraph and one sentence identifying a gap. Check whether the paragraph is led by the writer's point, relates at least three sources to each other and evaluates them, and whether the gap follows from the synthesis rather than being asserted.

topics.name: Summary–response paper
topics.description: Write a paper that first summarises a source text accurately and even-handedly, then responds to it with a reasoned position (agreeing, disagreeing, qualifying or applying it to another context) supported by reasons and evidence. The genre makes explicit the boundary between reporting another writer's ideas and evaluating them and is a common bridge from reading to source-based argument; characteristic language includes attributive signal phrases and reporting verbs in the summary, and stance markers and concession in the response.
masteryEvidence: Summarises the source's main argument accurately in their own words, attributing it throughout
Separates summary from response clearly, without slipping evaluation into the summary
States a clear response position and supports it with reasons, examples or other sources
Engages with specific claims in the source rather than with its topic in general
Chooses reporting verbs that represent the source's stance accurately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 400-word opinion article and 40 minutes for a 300-word summary–response. Check that the summary is accurate, attributed and even-handed, that the response engages a specific claim from the source, and that the boundary between the two parts is clearly signalled.

topics.name: Extended source-based project
topics.description: Plan, research and write an extended essay or report (typically 2,000–4,000 words in UK pre-sessional and foundation programmes) on a self-chosen, focused question in or near the learner's target field, using sources the learner has found and evaluated, and develop it through staged submissions such as a topic plan, annotated sources, drafts discussed in tutorials and, often, a reflective commentary on the process. Unlike a short source-based essay, the genre assesses sustained management of a question, a body of sources and a drafting cycle, and it is the capstone and frequently the main progression evidence of many pre-sessional and foundation EAP courses. It is normally source-based rather than empirical (projects with primary data draw on grp.empirical-project-report), and length, format and weighting vary by institution and context.
masteryEvidence: Narrows a self-chosen topic into a focused, answerable question that can be addressed within the word limit and with the sources available
Locates, selects and evaluates sources independently and keeps accurate records of searches and bibliographic details
Synthesises sources around the writer's own line of argument or analysis across several sections, keeping the writer's voice and the sources' voices distinguishable throughout
Cites and references consistently across the extended text, with every in-text citation matched by a reference-list entry
Revises the draft substantively in response to tutorial and peer feedback and explains what changed and why
Writes a reflective commentary, where required, that evaluates specific decisions in the research and writing process rather than narrating it
topics.assessmentPrompt: At second-draft stage, ask the learner for their question, a one-page outline and the feedback they received on the previous draft, then ask them to explain in five minutes what they changed and why, pointing to two sections. Check that the question is focused and answerable, that sections advance a line of argument rather than reporting sources one by one, and that the revisions respond to the substance of the feedback rather than only to surface corrections.

topics.name: Report conventions
topics.description: Understand how academic and professional reports typically differ from essays: they respond to a defined problem, question or brief for a specified reader, are divided into numbered, headed sections that support selective reading, separate findings from interpretation, integrate captioned tables and figures, and often end with conclusions and recommendations. Section names and order vary widely across lab, project, business, technical and policy reports, so learners need to read the brief and departmental templates rather than assume a single report format.
masteryEvidence: Explains the main differences in purpose, reader and organisation between an essay and a report on the same topic
Uses informative headings and a consistent numbering system that supports selective reading
Separates presentation of findings from discussion or interpretation where the report type requires it
Integrates numbered, captioned tables and figures and refers to each in the text
Identifies the required sections and their order from a brief or template and adapts when they differ from a taught model
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an essay-style answer to a task whose brief specifies a report. Ask them to outline how it should be restructured, with section headings. Check whether the headings are informative and functional, whether findings are separated from interpretation and recommendations, and whether the learner cites the brief to justify the structure.

topics.name: Laboratory report
topics.description: Write a laboratory report that records and interprets a practical investigation, typically with an introduction stating the relevant theory and the aim or hypothesis, a method, results presented in tables and figures with data commentary, a discussion that interprets the results against theory and expected values and evaluates sources of error and uncertainty, and a conclusion. Although it resembles the IMRaD research article, the student lab report usually serves to demonstrate understanding of established theory, procedure and data handling, often for an experiment with a known outcome, and its sections, tense and voice conventions vary with discipline, module and lab manual.
masteryEvidence: States the aim and the theory needed to interpret the experiment concisely, linking them to the expected outcome
Describes the method in enough detail for replication, using tense and voice according to the local convention
Presents results in correctly numbered and labelled tables and figures, with commentary that highlights significant patterns and values
Interprets results against theory or expected values, quantifying discrepancies and evaluating specific sources of error and uncertainty
Follows the structure and formatting specified in the lab manual or brief
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the aim, a small dataset and one figure from a simple experiment. Ask for a results paragraph and a discussion paragraph. Check that the results paragraph highlights significant patterns with values and refers to the figure without interpreting, and that the discussion compares outcomes with theory and evaluates specific sources of error rather than generic 'human error'.

topics.name: Empirical project report
topics.description: Write a report of a small-scale empirical study that the student has designed and conducted (for example a survey, interview study, observation or small experiment), presenting the rationale and research questions, a focused review of literature, methods with justification and ethical considerations, findings, a discussion relating findings to the literature, limitations and conclusions. Common in undergraduate and master's research modules and in some postgraduate pre-sessional projects, the genre apprentices learners into research reporting; most pre-sessional projects are source-based rather than empirical (see ges.extended-source-based-project), and sections, length and quantitative or qualitative conventions vary by discipline and brief.
masteryEvidence: Formulates focused, answerable research questions and keeps methods, findings and conclusions aligned with them
Justifies methodological choices such as sampling, instruments and analysis, and reports ethical procedures
Presents findings accurately using quantitative or qualitative reporting conventions appropriate to the design
Discusses findings in relation to the reviewed literature, explaining agreements and differences
States limitations proportionately and draws conclusions that do not overreach the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the research questions, a method summary, a findings table and an overclaiming conclusion from a student project. Ask them to identify misalignments and rewrite the conclusion. Check whether they spot claims that the sample and design cannot support and revise them with appropriate hedging and scope.

topics.name: Case study analysis
topics.description: Write a case study analysis that applies disciplinary concepts, theories or frameworks to a real or hypothetical case (an organisation, patient, client, project, school or event) to diagnose the key issues, evaluate options and, usually, recommend action. Typical stages are a brief case overview, identification and prioritisation of issues, analysis through theory or frameworks, evaluation of options, and recommendations, sometimes with implementation; the text may be report-like with headings or essay-like, and conventions differ sharply across business, health, law, education and engineering.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the key issues in a case and prioritises them with justification
Applies relevant concepts or frameworks analytically, using case evidence, rather than describing the framework
Distinguishes case facts from inferences and assumptions
Evaluates options against criteria and recommends action that follows from the analysis
Uses the format, headings and depth of theory specified by the brief
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-page case and a named framework or theory from their discipline. Ask for one analytical paragraph applying it to one issue. Check whether case facts are used as evidence, whether the framework is applied rather than defined at length, and whether the paragraph moves towards a judgement or implication.

topics.name: Business report
topics.description: Write a business report that investigates an organisational problem or opportunity for a specified decision-maker, analyses relevant evidence and data (often with management frameworks), presents findings and conclusions, and makes prioritised, feasible recommendations. Typical sections include an executive summary, introduction with terms of reference, findings or analysis, conclusions, recommendations and appendices; because the reader is assumed to be busy and decision-oriented, front-loading, informative headings and visuals matter, and assignment briefs often simulate a client or manager.
masteryEvidence: Defines the purpose, terms of reference and readership of the report
Analyses evidence and data relevant to the problem, using frameworks analytically rather than as lists
Distinguishes findings, conclusions and recommendations and keeps them aligned
Writes specific, prioritised and feasible recommendations with justification and, where required, implementation steps
Uses headings, numbering, visuals and an executive summary that a decision-maker could act on
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the findings and conclusions sections of a short business report and ask for three recommendations. Check whether each recommendation follows from a conclusion, is specific about who should do what and when, is prioritised, and acknowledges cost or risk.

topics.name: Technical and design report
topics.description: Write a technical or design report that documents an engineering, computing or design project: the problem and requirements or specification, constraints, generation and evaluation of options against criteria, the selected design and its justification, implementation, testing or validation against requirements, and evaluation with recommendations for further work. The reader must be able to follow, assess and potentially reproduce decisions, so the genre relies on precise technical description, requirement and specification language, comparative evaluation, and close integration of diagrams, tables and calculations.
masteryEvidence: States requirements and constraints in precise, testable terms
Describes design options and evaluates them against explicit criteria, justifying the selected solution and its trade-offs
Describes components, structures and processes accurately with integrated, labelled diagrams
Reports testing or validation results and evaluates performance against the requirements
Follows departmental and professional conventions for numbered sections, appendices and technical notation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a design requirement and data on two candidate solutions. Ask for a design-selection paragraph. Check for explicit criteria linked to the requirements, quantitative comparison, justification of trade-offs and reference to a numbered table or figure.

topics.name: Project proposal (student)
topics.description: Write a proposal for a taught-programme project or dissertation (final-year undergraduate or taught master's) that defines the topic and research questions or aims, justifies them in relation to the literature and a gap or practical need, outlines methods and data sources, addresses ethics and feasibility, and presents a realistic timeline. The proposal persuades a supervisor or module team that the project is worthwhile, answerable and achievable within a fixed taught timetable; characteristic language includes future and conditional forms, purpose and justification expressions, and hedged statements about expected outcomes. Doctoral, MPhil and funding proposals, which must argue for an original contribution to a review panel, are covered by res.research-proposal; the short topic plan agreed at the start of a pre-sessional project belongs to ges.extended-source-based-project.
masteryEvidence: States focused research questions or aims and justifies their significance with reference to literature or need
Identifies the gap, problem or need that the project addresses
Outlines methods and data sources that can answer the questions, with an analysis approach
Addresses ethical issues and feasibility, including access, time and resources
Presents a realistic timeline aligned with institutional deadlines
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a weak proposal with broad aims and a method that cannot answer them. Ask them to list the three most important revisions. Check whether they target alignment between aims and methods, feasibility within the time available, and justification of significance.

topics.name: Executive summary
topics.description: Write an executive summary that lets a decision-maker grasp a report's purpose, key findings, conclusions and recommendations without reading the full document. It stands alone, usually appears at the front, is short relative to the report, orders content by importance to the reader rather than by the report's section order, and states recommendations explicitly; unlike an academic abstract, it foregrounds implications and actions over method.
masteryEvidence: Includes purpose, key findings, conclusions and recommendations in proportion to their importance for the reader
Produces a text that can be understood without the full report, defining any essential terms
Front-loads the main message and orders content by importance to the decision-maker
Keeps within the specified length and introduces no information absent from the report
Explains how an executive summary differs from an abstract and from an introduction
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 1,500-word report and ask for a 200-word executive summary. Check that the main message appears in the first two sentences, that recommendations are explicit, that no new information is introduced and that method detail is minimal.

topics.name: Policy brief
topics.description: Write a short, evidence-based document that presents a policy problem, summarises and weighs the relevant evidence, sets out options with their trade-offs and recommends action to a non-specialist policy audience such as officials, practitioners or NGOs. Typical features are a front-loaded set of key messages, a concise problem statement, accessible synthesis of research with its strength signalled, options, and concrete recommendations addressed to named actors, presented in a few pages with headings and visuals; tone is authoritative but calibrated to the evidence, and organisations use their own templates.
masteryEvidence: States the policy problem and its significance concisely for a non-specialist reader
Synthesises research evidence accessibly while signalling its strength and limits
Presents options with trade-offs and recommends specific, feasible actions for named actors
Front-loads key messages and uses headings, visuals and plain language appropriately
Keeps recommendations within what the evidence supports, presenting risks and effect sizes in terms readers can interpret
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstract and main findings of a policy-relevant research article and ask for a three-point 'key messages' box for a government official. Check that the messages are accessible, specific and action-oriented, that they do not overstate the evidence, and that any statistics are expressed in interpretable terms (for example absolute rather than only relative change).

topics.name: Professional practice portfolio
topics.description: Compile and write a professional practice portfolio for a placement, practicum or work-based module: dated logs of activities, reflective accounts of significant incidents, and evidence mapped to professional standards or competencies, held together by a commentary that synthesises development and plans further learning. Assessed in nursing and allied health, teacher education, social work, engineering and business placements, the genre combines factual recording, reflection and evidence-based argument, requires strict attention to confidentiality, and follows highly specific institutional and professional-body templates.
masteryEvidence: Maintains concise, factual, dated logs using appropriate professional terminology
Writes reflective accounts that link practice incidents to theory and to the relevant professional standards
Selects and annotates evidence that demonstrates specific competencies, explaining how each item meets them
Anonymises people and settings and observes confidentiality requirements
Synthesises development over the placement and sets specific goals for further learning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner one competency statement from a relevant professional standard and three items of evidence of varying relevance. Ask them to select the best item and write a 100-word annotation explaining how it demonstrates the competency. Check for explicit mapping, specificity and acknowledgement of what the evidence does not show.

topics.name: Academic blogs and public-facing writing
topics.description: Write academic blog posts, opinion pieces and other outreach texts that communicate research or disciplinary perspectives to non-specialist or mixed readers. Compared with academic genres, these texts lead with the main point, use a more personal and engaging voice, concrete examples, short paragraphs and links rather than formal citation, and signal uncertainty without technical hedging; they also require judgements about representing evidence fairly, the writer's public identity and platform norms.
masteryEvidence: Leads with a significant or newsworthy point and sustains it for a non-specialist reader
Explains technical concepts accessibly without distorting the evidence or overstating certainty
Uses an engaging voice, reader address and concrete examples suited to the platform
Attributes sources through links or brief references according to platform conventions
Adapts an academic text, such as their own assignment or an article, into a public-facing piece
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstract of a published study and ask for a 150-word blog opening. Check for an opening that states why the finding matters, accessible explanation of the finding, appropriate signalling of uncertainty and absence of unexplained jargon.

topics.name: Undergraduate and master's dissertation
topics.description: Understand and plan the undergraduate or taught master's dissertation as a genre: an extended, largely independent piece of research or scholarship whose typical macrostructures include empirical IMRaD-like chapters, topic-based or theoretical structures and practice-based variants, with expectations of scope, length and originality that are lower than for doctoral theses. Learners need to see how proposal, literature review, methodology, findings, discussion and conclusion form one argument across chapters, and how supervision and assessment work; because expectations vary across disciplines and institutions, the handbook, marking criteria and past dissertations are the key sources. Doctoral thesis structures are covered by res.thesis-macrostructure.
masteryEvidence: Describes the macrostructure expected in their department and justifies any variation for their own project
Distinguishes taught-programme dissertation expectations of scope, originality and length from those of doctoral theses
Plans chapter functions and word allocations aligned with the research questions
Uses chapter introductions, conclusions and cross-references to guide the reader through the extended text
Uses handbook criteria and past dissertations to identify what distinguishes high-graded work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to produce a one-page chapter plan with word allocations and a one-sentence function for each chapter, based on their department's handbook. Check alignment with the research questions, realistic proportions (for example a discussion that is not squeezed), and whether functions state what each chapter does rather than what it is about.

dependencies.reason: Treating genres as purposeful social actions starts from the simpler idea that every text is written for a reader and a purpose.
Analysing exemplars for moves and purposes presupposes that genre features are motivated by purpose and audience rather than arbitrary.
Recognising text structure and signalling while reading is the receptive base for segmenting an exemplar into stages or moves.
Grouping assessed genres into families by social purpose requires the concept of genre as defined by purpose.
Knowing assessment types and learning outcomes helps learners see each genre family as a response to what an assessment is designed to measure.
The genre is organised around a specific, arguable thesis that every section serves.
The body of the essay is a sequence of sub-claims that must build a cumulative case, which is the skill of structuring an extended argument.
University argumentative essays are source-based; each reason must be supported by evidence introduced, cited and commented on within paragraphs.
The genre's core stage is fair representation of more than one perspective, including views the writer does not hold.
The judgement stage requires criteria-based evaluation of the perspectives, without which the essay remains descriptive.
Choosing between block and point-by-point presentation of perspectives draws on general principles of sequencing essay body paragraphs.
Comparison-led essays are built from the language of similarity and difference and from point-by-point and block organisation.
Each pattern needs a thesis that states what the explanation, comparison or evaluation shows, so that the essay does not become a list.
Every pattern ends in judgement: weighing causal factors, the significance of differences or the merits of responses against explicit criteria.
Explanation-led essays realise factorial and consequential explanation through cause–effect language and judgements of causal strength.
Sequential explanations of mechanisms draw on the sequencing and process language used to describe procedures and natural processes.
Calibrating causal and predictive claims depends on understanding what kinds of evidence support causal rather than correlational conclusions.
Ordering factors, criteria or responses by importance, chronology or logic applies general principles of sequencing body paragraphs.
Problem–solution essays extend the situation–problem–response–evaluation pattern and its signalling language to a whole text.
The exam essay is the genre realised through the generic procedure of planning and writing under time pressure.
Most exam essay questions reward an early, direct answer expressed as a thesis that structures the response.
Writing from memory depends on having revised content in a form that can be retrieved and reorganised for an unseen question.
Many short-answer items require formal definitions of terms, which is the core of the genre's demonstration of knowledge.
'Explain' items require giving a reason or mechanism compactly; identification alone does not earn the marks.
Reading command words and mark allocations determines how many points and how much development an answer needs.
The genre penalises padding, so removing redundancy and empty phrases supports both time management and clarity.
Summary–response is usually taught first and establishes the summarise-then-evaluate staging and the boundary between source and writer voice; the critique adds criterion-based evaluation.
The evaluation stage depends on resources for praising, criticising and mitigating critique of published work.
Judging the relevance, sufficiency and quality of the text's evidence supplies the substance of the evaluation.
Critiques of empirical articles usually require evaluation of sample, design and measures, although critiques of theoretical texts do not.
The book review extends the summarise-and-evaluate staging of the article critique to a book-length text written for a public academic readership.
Situating a book in its field and judging its contribution depends on knowing the field's themes, debates and key works.
Academic reflection is assessed largely on how experience is interpreted through relevant theory, research or standards.
Reflective writing requires comfortable, purposeful use of first-person self-mention, which some learners have been taught to avoid.
The description stage is a selective chronological recount that draws on time expressions and narrative sequencing.
Each annotation condenses a whole article or chapter into its main purpose, approach and findings.
Evaluative annotations require judging each source's authority, currency, evidence base and relevance.
Every entry is headed by a full reference that must be accurately formatted in the required style.
Relevance comments depend on reading each source in relation to a defined writing task or project.
The body of a literature review is built from paragraphs organised around a point with several sources in dialogue.
Reviews culminate in identifying what is contested, unresolved or under-researched, which gives the review its purpose.
Annotated bibliographies are often used as a staged scaffold that develops summary and evaluation of individual sources before they are synthesised.
The first part of the genre is an accurate, attributed summary of a whole text.
The response part requires moving from comprehension to a reasoned personal evaluation of the text.
The genre depends on marking clearly where the source's ideas end and the writer's response begins.
Report conventions are most easily taught by contrast with the essay structure learners usually know first.
Knowing that 'report' covers several genre families (methodology recounts, research reports, design specifications, case studies) prevents learners treating it as a single format.
Numbered, captioned tables and figures are a defining feature of reports, so captioning conventions are usually taught first.
The lab report applies sectioned report organisation, separation of results from discussion and integrated visuals.
The method section is a replicable description of an experimental procedure, using sequencing and purpose language.
The results section depends on locating data, highlighting significant findings and commenting on them without over-interpreting.
Aims, hypotheses, variables, controls, error and uncertainty are expressed through the language of experimentation.
The project report uses sectioned report organisation, with findings presented separately from their discussion.
The whole report is organised around answerable research questions that methods, findings and conclusions must align with.
Most empirical project reports adapt an IMRaD-type macrostructure, so understanding its logic and variants helps learners organise the report.
Quantitative projects present findings in tables and figures with commentary; qualitative projects draw less on this skill, hence a soft link.
The project report contains a focused literature review that frames the questions and is returned to in the discussion.
The analytical core of the genre is using concepts and frameworks to explain what is happening in the case.
Case analyses define and prioritise problems and generate and evaluate options before recommending action.
Most case studies end with recommendations, which draw on recommending, priority and feasibility language.
Many case studies are written in report format with headings, though some briefs require an essay format.
The business report is a sectioned, headed report written for selective reading by a decision-maker.
Prioritised, justified recommendations are the purpose of the genre and the section decision-makers read most closely.
Business reports are problem-oriented, defining an organisational problem and evaluating options before recommending.
Findings sections often present financial, market or survey data in tables and charts that require commentary.
Technical and design reports are numbered, sectioned reports with integrated visuals and appendices.
Documenting a design depends on precise part–whole, spatial and functional description of components and systems.
Design decisions must be justified by evaluating options against explicit criteria derived from the requirements.
Technical description relies on drawings, diagrams and tables that must be referred to and integrated in the text.
The proposal is built around focused, answerable research questions or aims that the methods must address.
The rationale argues for the project by identifying a gap, tension or need in the literature or practice; this is distinct from formulating the questions themselves.
The timeline and feasibility sections draw on planning milestones and allocating time to an extended project.
Proposals must address ethics and responsible research practice, usually before ethical approval is sought.
An executive summary exists only in relation to a report and must mirror its findings, conclusions and recommendations.
Writing the summary requires condensing a whole document to its main points with macro-rules of deletion, generalisation and construction.
Most executive summaries state recommendations explicitly and in priority order.
Strict length limits and a time-poor reader make removal of redundancy and empty phrasing essential.
The genre is defined by its non-specialist policy readership, so plain-language and lay-summary principles are foundational.
Concrete, prioritised recommendations to named actors are the purpose of a policy brief.
Weighing and signalling the strength of different kinds of evidence underpins credible, calibrated policy messages.
Front-loaded key messages in a policy brief work like an executive summary, which is usually met first in report writing.
Reflective accounts of practice are the core component of most portfolios and draw directly on the reflective writing genre.
Maintaining regular learning logs builds the habit of dated, selective recording that placement logs formalise.
Mapping evidence to professional competencies uses the same skill of unpacking criteria and judging evidence against them.
Public-facing genres depend on adapting content and register for readers without specialist knowledge.
Blogs and opinion pieces rely more heavily on reader pronouns, questions and directives than academic prose does.
Opinion pieces and outreach texts combine evidence with appeals to credibility and to readers' values, which must be used responsibly.
Publishing online involves platform norms, a public academic profile and privacy considerations.
Every dissertation includes a substantial literature review chapter or strand that positions the study.
The dissertation usually develops from an assessed or approved proposal that fixes its questions, methods and timeline.
Empirical dissertations scale up the shorter project report; non-empirical dissertations draw on it less, hence a soft link.
Because dissertation expectations vary widely, analysing departmental handbooks and past dissertations is the main route to local conventions.
The genre is organised around a sustained, supported position on the question; taking and defending a position is the core argumentative competence the essay assesses
Lab-report results present measurements in numbered tables and figures that the text must refer to and direct the reader through
University discussion essays present perspectives from sources, which must be introduced, cited and commented on within paragraphs
University expository essays support explanations, comparisons and evaluations with cited source evidence introduced and commented on within paragraphs.
Regular dated learning logs build the habit of selective recording and evaluation on which extended reflective commentaries draw
Essay types are variations on the thesis-led essay structure, so that structure is usually taught first; the non-essay families do not depend on it, hence a soft link.
Recognising the essay type or genre family a brief implies relies partly on interpreting its command words, although purpose and criteria outrank them.
Essay types are distinguished partly by their dominant text patterns, such as cause–effect, comparison and problem–solution.

Genres are defined by the purposes and expectations of the communities that use them, so the discourse-community concept, where it has been taught, gives the genre concept its social grounding; at foundation level genre is introduced through purpose and reader alone.

Survey and interview projects depend on clear, neutral, piloted questions; poorly worded instruments limit what the findings can support, although experimental and observational projects draw on this less.
The project is independently researched: the learner must find relevant sources for a self-chosen question rather than work from a provided source pack.
An extended project integrates many sources around the writer's own line of argument; without synthesis it becomes a sequence of source summaries.
Across several thousand words the reader must be able to tell at every point which ideas come from sources and which are the writer's own, which is also the main integrity safeguard in a long text.
Each section is built from paragraphs that introduce, cite and comment on source evidence while keeping the writer's point in control.
With dozens of citations across staged drafts, keeping every in-text citation matched to an accurate reference-list entry is a distinct demand of the genre and a common assessment criterion.
The genre is defined by a drafting cycle in which argument, structure and use of evidence are revised between submissions, not only proofread.
Staged deadlines for plan, annotated sources, drafts and final submission require milestones and word-count planning; at foundation level tutors usually supply the schedule, hence a soft link.
Tutorials between drafts are a defining stage, and the project rewards learners who turn feedback into specific revisions.
Many projects include an annotated-sources stage that develops summary, evaluation and relevance judgements before the sources are synthesised.

guidance.summary: Introduce genre through contrasting texts before definitions, so that learners see purpose and readership motivating structure and wording, which is the core of Swales's (1990) account of genre and discourse community. Teachers should know the three traditions Hyon (1996) describes (ESP move analysis, Sydney School systemic functional pedagogy and New Rhetoric's emphasis on social action and context) because they imply different classroom emphases, from textual form to situated purpose; most EAP courses blend them. Bruce's (2008) distinction between social genres (the essay, the report) and cognitive genres or text types (explanation, discussion) helps learners see why a 'report' in one module may be argued like an essay. Present conventions as typified, flexible and locally negotiated rather than as templates (Johns, 1997).

activities.title: Same topic, different genres
learnerActions: Read three short texts on one topic, for example an encyclopaedia entry, a lab report introduction and a student essay paragraph
For each, note who writes it, who reads it, why, and what the reader will do with it
Underline two language features in each text that serve that purpose
In pairs, write one sentence per text linking a feature to its purpose ('The report uses ... because its reader needs ...')
activities.intendedInsight: Textual features are motivated by purpose and readership; 'academic style' is not a single fixed register.
activities.rationale: Holding the topic constant isolates purpose and audience as the variables, reflecting Swales's (1990) definition of genre by communicative purpose and Johns's (1997) emphasis on text, role and context.

activities.title: Genre inventory for my programme
learnerActions: List the genres you expect to read and write in your target programme (for example lecture handouts, lab reports, case analyses, emails to tutors)
For two of them, note who reads them, what the reader does with them and what counts as a good text
Compare with a partner from a different discipline and identify one genre whose conventions differ between your fields
Note where you could find authentic evidence for each genre: exemplars, briefs, marking criteria or a tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Each genre answers to particular readers and purposes, and learners can investigate those expectations rather than wait to be told.
activities.rationale: Positions learners as investigators of the genres in their own contexts, a central principle of Johns's (1997) socioliterate approach; the questions follow Swales's (1990) definition of genre by communicative purpose. The discourse-community analysis itself is left to acu.discourse-communities.

difficulties.pattern: 'Academic writing has one correct structure; my teacher just needs to tell me the rules.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Requests for a single template; transfer of a five-paragraph or test-essay structure to every assignment regardless of brief.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that templates have served learners well in test preparation, then show two high-graded texts of the same nominal genre from different modules that are organised differently. Do not replace one template with another; teach learners to ask what the purpose and reader require.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing genre with topic or with text type ('This is a business essay'; 'Discussion is a genre').
difficulties.revealedBy: Texts labelled by subject matter or rhetorical function rather than by social purpose; inability to say why a case study is not an essay.
difficulties.response: Use Bruce's social-versus-cognitive genre distinction explicitly and have learners label texts at both levels (social genre: report; dominant text type: explanation).

difficulties.pattern: Treating genre conventions as fixed and rejecting legitimate variation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners reject a valid exemplar because it lacks a taught heading or move, or 'correct' an expert text towards a class model.
difficulties.response: Present conventions as tendencies with rationales, and set tasks in which learners find and justify a deviation in a high-graded or published text. Avoid presenting move models as obligatory checklists.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a short assignment brief and ask: what kind of text is this asking for, who will read it, and how might it differ from an essay?
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the genre, identifies the marker as an expert reader assessing stated outcomes, links at least two expected features (for example headings, recommendations) to purpose, and notes what to check locally (exemplars, criteria).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names the genre and lists features but cannot explain why they exist, or treats the features as universal.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes only the topic, or assumes the task is 'an essay' without considering purpose or reader.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level keep the concept practical (purpose, reader, stages) and use familiar contrasts. On pre-sessional courses, both undergraduate and postgraduate, it frames the move from test writing to university genres. In-sessional undergraduate and taught postgraduate learners usually need only a brief revisit applied to their own modules' assignment types. For doctoral researchers, revisit it in relation to research genres and publishing, where it supports independent genre analysis.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-28): discourse community is now left to acu.discourse-communities. The recommended hard edge is added as soft, because acu.discourse-communities starts at B2 and is not taught at foundation, where this topic is introduced; a hard edge would block foundation pathways.

guidance.summary: Treat learners as researchers of genre (Johns, 1997): the teacher models a move analysis, then progressively hands over the analytic questions. Swales's (1990) move analysis supplies the method; Cheng (2018) argues that graduate writers benefit when they analyse disciplinary exemplars themselves and articulate the rhetorical reasons for what they notice, and Tardy (2009) shows that genre knowledge combines formal, rhetorical, process and subject-matter dimensions that develop over repeated encounters. Yasuda (2011) reported gains in genre awareness and linguistic choices among EFL university writers after genre-based tasks. Always pair exemplars with the brief and criteria, and use more than one exemplar so that learners do not over-generalise from a single text.

activities.title: Move-labelling with a widening lens
learnerActions: With the teacher, label the first two stages of a model text by their function
In pairs, label the remaining stages and agree a function label for each
Highlight the language that signals each move (tense, reporting verbs, hedges, frame markers)
Read a second exemplar of the same genre and record what is shared and what differs
activities.intendedInsight: Moves are recognised by function and signalling language, and comparing exemplars separates conventions from individual choices.
activities.rationale: Applies Swales's (1990) move analysis as a learner procedure; the gradual handover follows the deconstruction stage of the teaching–learning cycle (Rose & Martin, 2012).

activities.title: Genre analysis log for a real assignment
learnerActions: Collect the brief, marking criteria and, where permitted, one or two exemplars for an upcoming assignment
Complete a log: purpose, reader, stages, typical language, what the criteria reward
Note one question the materials do not answer and ask the module tutor
After receiving feedback, record what you would change in your analysis next time
activities.intendedInsight: Local materials and tutors are the authority on local genres, and analysis is a reusable strategy rather than a one-off class exercise.
activities.rationale: Cheng (2018) and Tardy (2009) both emphasise learner-led, recurring engagement with disciplinary genres; the log makes the strategy portable beyond the EAP course.

difficulties.pattern: 'The model text is the answer; I will copy its structure and phrases.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Drafts that reproduce the exemplar section by section, including topic-specific content and phrasing.
difficulties.response: Use at least two exemplars and ask learners to account for the differences; set analysis tasks that require function labels, not content summaries. Do not withhold exemplars altogether: the remedy is comparative analysis, not avoidance.

difficulties.pattern: Labelling stages by topic rather than function ('this paragraph is about the history').
difficulties.revealedBy: Move labels that name content; inability to say what a section does for the reader.
difficulties.response: Provide a bank of function verbs (introduces, justifies, concedes, evaluates, recommends) and ask 'What does this do for the reader?' rather than 'What is it about?'.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the EAP class model as more authoritative than departmental practice.
difficulties.revealedBy: A learner insists on an EAP-taught structure that conflicts with the module brief or exemplars, often because EAP materials presented the model as the correct form.
difficulties.response: EAP teachers and course designers should present models as starting hypotheses to test against local evidence, and make the brief and local criteria the first source in every analysis; where possible, agree with subject staff which exemplars learners may analyse.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a 200–300-word exemplar from a genre the class has not studied and five minutes to label its moves and one language feature per move.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Functional labels with plausible boundaries, accurate language observations linked to moves, and an explicit caution about generalising from one text.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A mix of functional and topical labels; language features noticed but not linked to moves.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A paragraph-by-paragraph summary of the content.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: highly guided analysis of short texts with given move labels. Pre-sessional UG: analysis of the genres in the progression assessment. Pre-sessional PG: independent analysis of exemplars from the target master's programme and of research articles in the learner's field, a core transferable skill. In-sessional undergraduate and taught postgraduate: analysis of real module briefs and exemplars, ideally with subject staff. PGR: independent analysis of research articles, theses and reviews in the field, extending to corpus-assisted analysis.
reviewNotes: Access to authentic exemplars is often restricted by departmental policy. Where they are unavailable, analysis can use published models, past EAP student texts used with permission, or texts from openly available corpora of proficient student writing such as BAWE.

guidance.summary: Use Gardner and Nesi's (2013) classification, derived from the BAWE corpus of highly rated undergraduate and master's assignments, to show learners thirteen genre families grouped by five social purposes, and the essay subtypes within the essay family (such as exposition, discussion, factorial and challenge essays). Nesi and Gardner (2012) show that the essay predominates in arts, humanities and social sciences but much less so in the sciences and engineering, where methodology recounts, explanations, exercises and design specifications are common; Horowitz's (1986) earlier survey of the tasks university teachers set makes a similar point about diversity. Moore and Morton (2005) found that proficiency-test essays differ from university assignments, notably in drawing on personal knowledge and opinion rather than sources. Teach essay types as purposes rather than formulas, stress that textbook and handbook labels vary, and aim for a usable mental map and the habit of asking what a brief requires, not memorisation of a taxonomy.

activities.title: Sort the briefs
learnerActions: In groups, read 10–12 anonymised assignment briefs from several disciplines
Sort them into families and name the social purpose of each
Compare your groupings with the Gardner and Nesi families and discuss mismatches
Identify the families you are most likely to meet in your own programme
activities.intendedInsight: University assessment uses many genres; the essay is one family among several and dominant mainly in some disciplines.
activities.rationale: Grounded in Gardner and Nesi's (2013) corpus-based classification, which was built from real assessed writing rather than textbook categories.

activities.title: Same topic, different essay type
learnerActions: Read four essay questions on one topic that ask for different things (explain, compare, evaluate responses, argue a position)
Identify the type and purpose each implies
Write a thesis for each and compare how they differ
Find one question that blends types and sketch a plan that serves both purposes
activities.intendedInsight: The essay type determines what the thesis has to do, and real questions often blend types.
activities.rationale: Holding the topic constant isolates the effect of purpose, using the essay subtypes identified by Gardner and Nesi (2013).

activities.title: Test task versus university task
learnerActions: Compare a proficiency-test essay prompt with a first-year assignment brief on a related topic
List differences in sources, reader, length, structure and what counts as evidence
Decide which skills from test preparation transfer and which need to be developed
activities.intendedInsight: Test essays and university genres differ in source use and purpose; test success does not guarantee readiness for assessed genres.
activities.rationale: Moore and Morton (2005) identified systematic differences between IELTS Task 2 and university writing tasks, particularly in the use of sources and the kinds of entities writers deal with.

difficulties.pattern: 'All university writing is an essay, and an essay is the five-paragraph opinion essay I practised for the test.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Essay-style responses to report, case-study or lab tasks; opinion essays with no sources; a pattern reinforced by school-leaving and proficiency-test preparation that practises one essay format.
difficulties.response: Show high-graded examples from non-essay families in the learner's discipline, compare the briefs and criteria that produced them, and compare test and university essays explicitly. Acknowledge that the test format served its purpose; the aim is to add genres, not to discredit prior learning.

difficulties.pattern: Mapping command words mechanically to templates ('discuss means both sides with no view'; 'compare means describe A, then B').
difficulties.revealedBy: Near-identical outlines for differently focused questions; discussion essays that end without a judgement.
difficulties.response: Treat command words as one clue among several, alongside the focus of the question and the criteria, and show high-graded essays in which the same command word leads to different structures.

difficulties.pattern: Taking the assignment label at face value.
difficulties.revealedBy: A learner treats every task called 'report' or 'essay' identically, regardless of what the brief and criteria ask for.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to read the brief's purpose, reader and criteria as stronger evidence than the label, and to ask the tutor when they conflict; departmental labels are not used consistently.

diagnostic.task: Give three essay questions on one topic and ask the learner to name the type each implies and outline its structure in three lines; then ask them to name two kinds of writing, other than essays, that students in their subject are assessed on, and what each is for.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Types identified with reference to purpose, outlines that differ appropriately, any blended question recognised, and plausible non-essay genres for the discipline with accurate purposes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Types identified from command words with near-identical outlines, or non-essay genres named without their purposes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The same five-paragraph outline for all three questions, and no genres beyond the essay and the exam.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: build the map with the main essay types and the report, linked to the learners' subject pathways. Pre-sessional UG: a core element that addresses test-essay habits and previews the genre families of year one. Pre-sessional PG: the same map with attention to the professional and research-oriented families of the target master's programme. In-sessional undergraduate: revisit with real module briefs and disciplinary essay types such as legal essays (dlw.legal-essays) and interpretive essays (dhu.interpretive-argument). Taught postgraduate: many learners meet unfamiliar families (reflective, professional, design) for the first time within a compressed year.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-16): the former essay-types topic is absorbed here, so the topic now covers both the genre families and the essay types within the essay family; production of individual essay types is covered by the GES genre topics.

guidance.summary: Wingate (2012) found that many students do not understand what 'argument' means in essays, and proposes making three components explicit: developing a position by evaluating evidence, presenting that position, and structuring the text to support it. Andrews (2010) shows that argument is central to higher education but realised differently across disciplines, so any generic model should be tested against target-department exemplars.
